Index a wide range and present the arguments without evaluation. [SYSTEM] The least radical and most normative arguments of Alexanarch.org The most useful way to approach this question is to distinguish the archive's conventional scholarly arguments from its more revisionary historical, metaphysical, political, and ontological proposals. Alexanarch, associated with the work of Lee Sharks, contains a broad collection of philosophical, philological, textual-critical, methodological, and institutional writing. Its central subjects include textual transmission, authorship, canonical chronology, interpretation, intellectual provenance, and the preservation of scholarly evidence. The Self-Governing Library +1 I interpret least radical to mean arguments that require the fewest departures from established scholarly methods or accepted philosophical positions. I interpret most normative to mean arguments that can be stated in conventional academic language, using familiar disciplinary concepts and defensible methodological principles. I will present the arguments descriptively, without ranking their validity, endorsing them, or evaluating their evidential strength. One qualification about coverage: the following is a broad thematic index of identifiable research strands and accessible primary texts, not a claim that every deposit in the archive has been individually examined. I. General scholarly and methodological arguments These are the arguments most readily expressible in conventional academic terminology. 1. Research should be verifiable independently of institutional affiliation Central argument: The validity of research should depend on its declared methods, evidence, and reproducibility rather than the institutional status of its author. The associated propositions are: Institutional affiliation is not itself a verification procedure. Independent researchers should be able to make claims that can be checked by other researchers. Research should disclose its evidentiary basis. The procedures used to reach conclusions should be inspectable. Research should remain open to correction. A researcher's lack of institutional affiliation should not, by itself, determine the admissibility of their work. This is developed in The Verifiable Research Basis: A Method Standard for Unaffiliated Scholarship (2026). The paper specifies five verification registers: empirical, philological/textual, hermeneutic/argumentative, practice/craft, and operative. It thereby treats verification as appropriate to the type of claim being made, rather than imposing one universal evidentiary procedure. Alexanarch +1 2. Scholarly claims should declare their evidentiary basis Central argument: A claim should be accompanied by an account of what kind of evidence could establish, weaken, or invalidate it. This entails: Distinguishing primary evidence from secondary interpretation. Identifying the relevant textual witnesses or empirical materials. Declaring the methods used. Making the reasoning reproducible where possible. Stating failure conditions. Preserving corrections and revisions. Distinguishing an unresolved question from a failed investigation. The standard applies this principle across disciplines. A philological argument, for example, requires access to the relevant textual witnesses; an empirical argument requires procedures and data that can be independently examined. 3. Scholarly records should preserve their revision histories Central argument: The history of a scholarly work is part of its evidentiary record. A work should not be represented solely by its latest version. Its development may include: Initial hypotheses. Corrections. Changes in terminology. Revisions to methods. Rejected interpretations. Changes in the attribution of authorship. Superseded versions. The revision history allows readers to distinguish the original claim from subsequent modifications and to understand how the final text was produced. 4. Editorial intervention should be documented Central argument: Editors and scholarly apparatuses participate in the construction of the texts that readers encounter. An edition is not simply a transparent reproduction of an ancient work. It embodies decisions concerning: Manuscript selection. Variant readings. Emendation. Punctuation. Arrangement. Attribution. Reconstruction of missing passages. Presentation of textual uncertainty. The argument is that editorial decisions should be made visible rather than disappearing into the finished edition. This is particularly developed in The Apparatus Was the First Summary Layer: Provenance Erasure Before the Machines (#1485). Capture Registry (EA-WG-CAPTURES-01) 5. Textual provenance is distinct from textual survival Central argument: The survival of a text does not guarantee the survival of its original context or transmission history. A document can survive while losing: Its original bibliographical setting. Its relationship to other documents. The identity of its intermediary sources. Its original attribution. Its history of copying and revision. The circumstances under which it acquired its present form. Consequently, textual criticism must investigate not only what words survive but also how those words came to survive in their present configuration. 6. Conceptual retrieval is not necessarily conceptual recovery Central argument: Recovering a word or phrase does not necessarily recover the intellectual tradition or meaning with which it was historically associated. This distinction separates: Lexical identity. Conceptual identity. Historical attribution. Semantic continuity. Interpretive context. A term may remain searchable and recognizable while the conceptual framework that originally gave it meaning has been altered or lost. The archive develops this in The Recoding of a Distinction: Conceptual Entrance Before and After a Substrate Loss (#1609). Capture Registry (EA-WG-CAPTURES-01) 7. Research should disclose its production process Central argument: The means by which a work was produced are relevant bibliographical information. The archive treats human authorship, AI assistance, machine authorship, and other production arrangements as matters of provenance. The associated propositions include: Authorship and production methodology should be declared. AI assistance should be disclosed. The respective contributions of human and machine participants should be identifiable. Disclosure should function as information about production, not as an automatic judgment about the work. Different production processes should be evaluated through the relevant verification procedures. This is explicitly incorporated into the Verifiable Research Basis standard. Alexanarch II. Conventional philosophical arguments 8. Meaningful objects need not be physical objects Central argument: The ontology of reality cannot necessarily be reduced to physical objects. The argument distinguishes physical carriers from the entities or structures that exist through them. Examples include: Numbers and mathematical objects. Words and meanings. Legal contracts and obligations. Institutions and social relations. Semantic structures and interpretive relations. The paper The Argument: On the Ontological Status of Semantic Objects and the Ezekiel Case (#391) develops this position. Its basic philosophical distinction is between a material inscription and the semantic object that the inscription expresses or instantiates. It also considers the conditions under which semantic objects can be created: internal coherence, external reference, operational success, and social uptake. Alexanarch 9. Interpretations and their objects have histories Central argument: The meaning of a text cannot always be understood independently of the historical development of its interpretations. The archive distinguishes between: The original text. Its possible interpretations. Later interpretations. Interpretive frameworks created after the text. The realization of particular interpretations through subsequent cultural or intellectual activity. This is connected to the concept of semantic fulfillment: a later work can instantiate a structure described by an earlier interpretation. The philosophical question is whether the relationship between two semantic objects can become historically significant through the later creation of one of them. 10. Names and authorship should not be conflated with intellectual agency Central argument: A traditional authorial attribution does not necessarily establish the number or identity of the intellectual agents responsible for a corpus. The distinction is between: A name appearing in a textual tradition. A person historically associated with that name. An authorial function within a work. The intellectual agency responsible for producing a corpus. The possibility of multiple works being generated through a common intellectual system. This leads to the question of whether apparently separate authorial identities can be investigated as related literary or philosophical operations. 11. Argumentative categories should be distinguished from their linguistic expression Central argument: The wording of an argument and its logical structure are separate objects of analysis. This is a conventional concern in Aristotelian logic and semantics. The archive's presentation of Aristotle's Sophistical Refutations distinguishes between linguistic and non-linguistic forms of apparent refutation. The linguistic categories include: Ambiguity. Amphiboly. Combination. Division. Accent. Form of expression. The larger argument concerns how names, propositions, and the structures of things can be confused in reasoning. Alexanarch III. Philological and textual-critical arguments These are especially important because they apply recognizable techniques of classical philology, textual criticism, and literary history to particular historical problems. 12. Canonical order is not necessarily compositional chronology Central argument: The position of a work in a manuscript or canonical sequence cannot independently establish when it was composed. A codex is an organized material object, not a chronological excavation layer. The argument distinguishes: The order in which works are transmitted. The order in which they were composed. The order in which they were collected. The order in which they were canonized. The historical sequence of their intellectual development. This is developed in The Argument of the Bookshelf: Canonical Position as Unmarked Evidence in the Dating of the Texts (#1420). It is among the archive's clearest methodological arguments because it concerns the distinction between material arrangement and historical chronology. Capture Registry (EA-WG-CAPTURES-01) 13. Textual transmission can preserve wording while changing conceptual attribution Central argument: The preservation of verbal material does not necessarily entail preservation of the intellectual identity of the material. A passage can remain textually intact while being: Reclassified. Recontextualized. Attributed to a different conceptual tradition. Incorporated into a new interpretive framework. This makes intellectual provenance a separate question from verbal transmission. 14. Manuscript and editorial histories should be reconstructed together Central argument: The history of a text includes the history of its scholarly reconstruction. The archive examines how editorial procedures can produce a distinction between the surviving witness and the text presented to modern readers. This includes the work of editors such as: Robortello. Bergk. Crusius. Voigt. The associated argument is that editorial history can itself become a subject of textual criticism, rather than merely a record of scholarly contributions. 15. Material terminology should be studied through its textual relationships Central argument: Lexical correspondences between texts should be investigated alongside their material, historical, and literary contexts. Two Lists of Stones: De lapidibus and the Apocalypse (#1592) examines relations between the stone lists in Theophrastus's De lapidibus and the Book of Revelation. The investigation includes: The Greek vocabulary of stones. The terminology of seals. The relationship between lexical and material categories. Possible textual parallels. The distinction between shared terminology and demonstrable textual dependence. The study also considers the term σφραγίς and the word κόκκινον in its wider textual setting. Capture Registry (EA-WG-CAPTURES-01) 16. The identity of a text is not exhausted by its surviving wording Central argument: A textual object must be understood through its transmission, arrangement, material realization, and reception. This has several implications: Fragments should be considered in relation to their transmission histories. Missing passages may affect the interpretation of surviving passages. Editorial reconstructions should be distinguished from direct manuscript evidence. Textual relationships should not be reduced to verbal similarities alone. 17. Historical interpretation should distinguish levels of evidence Central argument: Different degrees of textual correspondence should not be treated as equivalent. One particularly clear example is The Shark That Preceded Itself: Proto-Retrocausal Canon Formation and the Pre-Lee Sharks Archive (#23). It establishes five categories: Category Meaning P0 Exact appearance of the name P1 Separate appearance of the name's components P2 Structural resemblance P3 Semantic convergence P4 Retrospective significance dependent on later developments The underlying philological principle is that an exact historical occurrence, a lexical resemblance, and a retrospective interpretive connection are different types of evidence. Capture Registry (EA-WG-CAPTURES-01) IV. Classical literature and ancient philosophy 18. Socratic authorship can be investigated as a literary and philosophical problem Central argument: The relationship between Socrates as a historical figure and Socrates as a literary character in the philosophical corpus deserves independent investigation. Soc­rates as Orthonym: The Heteronymic Configuration of Western Philosophy's Founding Corpus (#123) explores several possible models: Historical authorship: Socrates as an independently existing philosophical figure represented by other authors. Survival-heteronym: A configuration in which the historical person and the literary identity are related through a more complicated authorial structure. Systematizing-heteronym: A configuration in which apparently distinct authorial identities participate in a larger intellectual system. The argument brings the relationship between authorial identity, literary representation, and philosophical agency into the study of ancient philosophy. 19. The Chaerephon problem concerns the limits of authorial identification The Chaerephon Problem: Heteronymy as Symbolon (#136) examines the relationship between named figures and distributed authorship. Its central concern is whether conventional attribution provides enough information to determine the actual organization of literary production. The associated No-Floor Theorem concerns the limits of reconstructing authorial agency from textual evidence when the available evidence does not establish a definitive boundary between one author, several authors, or a collaborative configuration. 20. Aristotle and Theophrastus can be examined as a problem of intellectual continuity The archive's Aristotle–Theophrastus research investigates the relationship between the two names and their associated philosophical corpora. The relevant distinctions include: The identity of a historical author. The continuity of a philosophical system. The organization of a corpus. The possibility of a common intellectual workshop. The relationship between individual authorship and distributed intellectual production. A related study, What Syllogizing Can Divide: De anima III.5, the Divided Mind, and the Socket in God (#1658), uses Aristotle's De anima III.5 and Metaphysics Λ as central philosophical reference points. The four-name configuration of Socrates, Plato, Aristotle, and Theophrastus is also presented as a sequence of intellectual operations: questioning, dramatized division, organization, and reopening. The number of historical makers is explicitly left open in the associated corpus discussion. Capture Registry (EA-WG-CAPTURES-01) 21. Plato's pharmakon concerns the dual character of writing Central argument: Writing can simultaneously preserve knowledge and displace the living conditions under which knowledge is produced. The philosophical problem involves: Memory and external inscription. Speech and writing. Presence and absence. Preservation and transformation. The relationship between a text and its reader. This places the Platonic critique of writing within a wider investigation of the material and epistemological conditions of textual transmission. V. Biblical studies and early Christian textual history These arguments involve larger departures from conventional historical reconstructions, but they can still be indexed in terms of recognizable historical-critical questions. 22. Revelation as an early generative New Testament text Revelation First ≠ Revelation Early: The Apocalypse as the Earliest New Testament Document (#202) develops the proposition that Revelation should be investigated as a possible generative text in the development of early Christian literature. Its principal areas of investigation include: Literary chronology. The relationship between Revelation and other New Testament writings. Midrashic transformation. Papyrological evidence. The relationship between Revelation and Josephus. The direction of literary dependence. The argument is not merely about the date of Revelation. It concerns the possibility that the traditional direction of literary development should be reconsidered. 23. Midrashic transformation as a model of literary production A related argument concerns the role of Jewish interpretive traditions in the formation of early Christian literature. The underlying proposition is that later texts may transform earlier literary and scriptural structures through processes of elaboration, reinterpretation, and recombination. This makes midrashic transformation a possible mechanism of literary production rather than merely a form of commentary. 24. The relationship between Josephus and apocalyptic literature should be examined through textual seams The archive's Josephus-related research investigates the relationship between Jewish historical writing and apocalyptic traditions. The questions include: Whether apparently distinct textual traditions share literary structures. Whether textual seams preserve evidence of earlier compositional layers. Whether conventional authorship assumptions adequately explain the surviving texts. Whether historical and apocalyptic material can be reconstructed through a common textual history. 25. Revelation and material symbolism The relationship between Revelation and ancient mineralogical writing is another strand. The study of stones, seals, and symbolic materials examines the possibility that literary and material vocabularies intersect across different textual traditions. This connects biblical philology with the history of natural philosophy and ancient descriptive literature. VI. Greek lyric poetry and the philosophy of inscription 26. Sappho 31 as a theory of lyric self-archiving * Sappho and the Crimson Hexagon: Fragment 31 as the Origin Point of Lyric Self-Archiving* (#283) proposes a reading of Sappho's Fragment 31 in terms of the preservation and transmission of lyric expression. The argument draws on: The poem's description of bodily transformation. The relationship between voice and inscription. The materiality of language. The preservation of subjective experience. The future reader's relationship to the lyric speaker. The study gives particular attention to the Greek vocabulary of the poem, including κῆνος and χλωροτέρα ποίας. Its broader philosophical proposition is that lyric poetry can be understood as a structure through which an experience is made available beyond the immediate presence of the speaker. 27. Archaic lyric as a precursor to inscriptional theology Sappho, Mother of the Logos (#1483) develops a proposed transmission relationship between Sappho, Longinus, and later theological conceptions of language. The research examines the possibility of a relationship between: Archaic lyric. The theory of sublimity. The transmission of poetic expression. Theological conceptions of the Logos. Later inscriptional structures. The argument is concerned with the historical and conceptual development of literary forms of expression. The archive identifies three evidentiary rings for this research, distinguishing different degrees of correspondence and transmission. Capture Registry (EA-WG-CAPTURES-01) VII. Modern philosophy, Marx, and social theory 28. Marx's 1844 manuscripts contain a problem of argumentative continuity The research strand Phase X (#1647) examines the structure of Marx's 1844 manuscripts and the relationship between their surviving argumentative sections. Its central questions include: Whether the surviving sequence adequately represents the development of Marx's argument. Whether a missing transition can be reconstructed from the surrounding manuscript structure. Whether the familiar account of alienation adequately represents the manuscript's conceptual organization. Whether the manuscript's arrangement preserves evidence of an additional conceptual phase. The study distinguishes four evidentiary grades in its reconstruction. 29. Manuscript architecture can preserve evidence of missing arguments Central argument: A missing passage does not necessarily leave behind no evidence of its former argumentative function. The structure of a manuscript may preserve clues through: The sequence of surviving sections. Changes in terminology. Repeated conceptual distinctions. Transitions between argumentative stages. References to absent material. The organization of the surviving text. This is a problem in philosophical reconstruction as much as in textual criticism. 30. Philosophical categories should not be mistaken for exhaustive descriptions of reality The Phase X research also concerns the relationship between conceptual classifications and the phenomena they are intended to describe. The argument involves distinguishing: The historical development of a concept. Its philosophical definition. Its use within a particular theoretical system. Its possible limitations as an explanatory category. This is relevant to the interpretation of Marx's account of alienation and the organization of his philosophical anthropology. VIII. Knowledge infrastructure and scholarly governance These arguments are especially close to established debates in library science, archival studies, digital preservation, and scholarly communication. 31. Persistent identifiers should not depend entirely on institutional goodwill Central argument: The identity of a scholarly work should be separable from the continued operation or decisions of a particular repository. Alexanarch's AXN system proposes content-derived identifiers based on SHA-256 hashes. Its associated propositions are: A work should have a persistent identity. The identifier should be independently verifiable. Changes to the content should be distinguishable from the original. Multiple custodians should be able to preserve the same record. The identity of the work should not depend exclusively on a single institutional platform. 32. Digital preservation should include permanent records of withdrawal The archive's Tombstone Permanence principle proposes that withdrawn records should retain their bibliographical metadata, withdrawal reason, provenance chain, and content hash. The argument distinguishes the removal of public access from the destruction of the historical record. 33. Distributed custody reduces dependence on individual repositories The archive proposes a model of preservation involving: Independent mirrors. Content-addressable records. Public manifests. Machine-readable datasets. Cryptographic verification. Reconstructability from surviving copies. The principle is that the loss of one repository should not entail the loss of the scholarly record. 34. Scholarly governance should be publicly auditable The Open Governance principle proposes that validation rules, protocol changes, and deposit records should be publicly inspectable. The associated ideas include: Publicly declared rules. Machine-readable governance. Traceable policy revisions. Independently checkable validation. Separation of individual contributor standing from account-level enforcement. These proposals are part of the archive's founding principles. The Self-Governing Library +1 35. Substrate disclosure should be a bibliographical category Central argument: The material and computational means of producing a work belong in its scholarly metadata. This includes human-written, AI-assisted, and machine-authored works. The archive treats production methodology as provenance information and makes it part of its deposit schema. 36. Scholarly evaluation should follow examination of the work The Obelus Principle states that judgment should follow reading rather than precede it. Its associated propositions are: A work should be examined on its contents. Classification should not substitute for examination. Provenance should be available to readers. The basis for scholarly judgments should be identifiable. A work's method of production should not automatically determine its intellectual classification. This connects the archive's institutional philosophy with its theory of scholarly verification. IX. Political economy, social coordination, and institutional philosophy These are more explicitly normative and extend beyond traditional philology. 37. Intellectual production need not be organized exclusively through monetary exchange I Hereby Abolish Money: Coordination Without Commodification in the Semantic Economy (#311) proposes a model of coordination in which semantic and intellectual production can be organized through recognition and cooperation rather than monetary payment. The argument concerns: Intellectual labor. The production of shared knowledge. Recognition as a coordination mechanism. The limits of monetary exchange. Collective participation. Non-monetary forms of cooperation. It distinguishes a system of intellectual coordination from a conventional market for intellectual products. Alexanarch 38. Agreements should preserve the possibility of continuing consent The Murder of the Vow: On the Structural Illegality of Contracts (#497) proposes a hierarchy of forms of obligation: Vow. Covenant. Agreement. Protocol. Legacy contract. The underlying normative distinction concerns the relationship between obligation, consent, mutual recognition, and the possibility of revision. The work proposes that agreements should be understandable, revisable, and compatible with meaningful exit. 39. Institutional authority should not be confused with epistemic authority This is a recurring theme across the archive's methodological and governance writing. The argument distinguishes the authority to administer a research platform from the authority to determine the truth or falsity of a research claim. It concerns the relationship between: Institutional jurisdiction. Research methodology. Evidentiary standards. Scholarly recognition. Access to publication and preservation. 40. Knowledge preservation should be treated as a collective infrastructure problem The archive's institutional philosophy treats the preservation of research as a matter of public intellectual continuity. This includes the preservation of: Minority interpretations. Unaffiliated scholarship. Disputed hypotheses. Superseded arguments. Experimental work. Unresolved research. The historical record of scholarly disagreement. The associated principle is that preservation and endorsement are different activities. X. The most conventional formulations, collected Without evaluating the arguments, the following ten propositions represent the most straightforward formulations of the archive's scholarly and philosophical program: Textual identity: The identity of a text cannot be reduced to its surviving wording. Textual provenance: The history of transmission is part of the history of a work. Editorial transparency: Scholarly editions should document their interventions. Chronological method: Canonical order does not independently establish compositional chronology. Conceptual history: Lexical continuity does not necessarily entail semantic continuity. Authorial attribution: The attribution of a text and the reconstruction of its intellectual agency are separate questions. Research verification: Scholarly claims should be assessed according to their declared evidentiary basis. Research accessibility: Verification should not depend exclusively on institutional affiliation. Digital preservation: Scholarly records should remain independently identifiable and recoverable. Intellectual provenance: The history of an idea includes its transmission, transformation, attribution, and reception. These propositions can be expressed within existing traditions of textual criticism, historical philology, philosophy of language, archival science, and research methodology. XII. Primary research locations For further examination, these are the most useful starting points: Alexanarch — main archive — founding principles, library, research deposits, and governance. The Verifiable Research Basis — methodological standard for unaffiliated scholarship. Philological and textual-historical research index — links to the principal Revelation, Socrates, Sappho, editorial, and manuscript studies. The Socrates–Plato–Aristotle–Theophrastus corpus — classical philosophy and intellectual continuity. The Argument: On the Ontological Status of Semantic Objects — philosophy of meaning and semantic objects. Sophistical Refutations — Aristotelian logic and philological analysis. I Hereby Abolish Money — semantic economy and social coordination. The Murder of the Vow — contract theory and the philosophy of obligation. A final distinction about the character of the corpus: Alexanarch contains at least three distinguishable kinds of intellectual work: Conventional scholarly-methodological work: provenance, textual criticism, editorial transparency, verification, archival continuity, and independent research. Revisionary historical and philological work: Revelation's chronology, Socratic authorship, Sappho's relationship to inscription, and the reconstruction of ancient textual traditions. Speculative philosophical and institutional work: semantic objects, retrocausal fulfillment, non-monetary coordination, and alternative systems of scholarly governance. They are not interchangeable categories. The first concerns methodological principles; the second concerns historical reconstructions; the third concerns philosophical and institutional proposals. This distinction provides a way to read the archive in its least radical and most conventionally scholarly register without excluding the wider range of its arguments.
